edits.source_excerpt: On a Jordan block $J_\lambda=\lambda I+N$ with nilpotent $N$, one has $$J_\lambda^k=\sum_{j=0}^{s-1}\binom{k}{j}\lambda^{k-j}N^j.$$ Because $|\lambda|<1$, each scalar factor $\binom{k}{j}\lambda^{k-j}$ tends to $0$, so every Jordan block tends to $0$.
edits.proposed_replacement: On a Jordan block $J_\lambda=\lambda I+N$ of size $s$, one has $N^s=0$ and, for $k\ge s$, the finite binomial expansion gives $$J_\lambda^k=\sum_{j=0}^{s-1}\binom{k}{j}\lambda^{k-j}N^j.$$ If $\lambda=0$, then $J_0^k=N^k=0$ for $k\ge s$. If $0<|\lambda|<1$, each scalar factor $\binom{k}{j}\lambda^{k-j}$ tends to $0$: for fixed $j$, its absolute value is bounded by a constant times $k^j|\lambda|^k$, whose successive-term ratio tends to $|\lambda|<1$. Thus every Jordan block tends to $0$.
